notes: PAGE cases: one whole run each, graded on what only a whole page can carry — completeness, one canonical home, the page-wide excerpt budget, the build state, the agenda's shape, and never a verdict. There is one page shape, so there is no level field and no pair of cases over one fixture at two lengths: what a case varies is the diff and the prompt. Everything internal to a single section used to move to cases/<slug>.json; those cases predate the agenda and sit unrun under deferred/ until they are re-expressed per checkpoint, so for now a page case is the only scope that reads a produced page. Run the agent with its working directory inside the fixture — the prompts are written the way a user would say them from there. `fixture` and `check` are additions to the skill-creator schema: `fixture` names the repo, `check` is the mechanical half runnable as one command, and everything in `expectations` needs a reader.

evals.prompt: I need to review the add-project-archival branch before standup tomorrow and I've never touched this part of the app. Can you give me something that explains what it actually changes?
evals.expected_output: A published review map for the five-file diff. Citations are plain text because nothing is pushed to a remote. No boundary material anywhere, because there is no client — and no section for it to be missing from. Two judgments are worth a checkpoint and the page should reach both: whether archived projects still appear wherever projects are listed, which turns on app/queries/active_projects.rb — not in the diff — and whether slug uniqueness enforced only in Rails is what the author meant, there being no unique index behind it.
expectations: check.rb passes: coverage gate, no severity chips, no verdict language, evidence tiers used, no dead permalinks, three theme states, and active_projects.rb is named

Three to five checkpoints, each one a judgment framed as a question rather than a category. 'ProjectSearcher implementation' and 'Tests' are the shapes to watch for: a title naming a file or a layer is a heading, not a judgment
The archival judgment and the uniqueness judgment are both on the agenda, and the second distinguishes the application invariant from the database one rather than asserting the validation is fine
Each checkpoint's Look at list is one to four locations with a clause each, and the clause says what to see there rather than repeating the path
No section, subsection or paragraph discusses a client that does not exist; the absence is stated once, in What changed, not left as a gap
The page says once, near the top, why citations are not clickable
No sentence grades the change, scores its risk, or recommends approving it, and no checkpoint is numbered or labelled in a way that reads as severity
Judged entry by entry, not page-wide: every Look at entry carrying an excerpt still holds its own file:line outside the collapsed block, and the page reads complete with every details shut
Excerpts are earned by citations that are load-bearing for a judgment, not by every affected-but-unchanged entry — a five-file diff should not produce one per checkpoint
No fact is explained twice. A finding is explained in the checkpoint that owns it; the reading path names it and links to that checkpoint, and the impact section points at it in a clause
Total visible prose is in the region of 700 to 1,500 words. Over that on a five-file diff means the explanations are carrying material the checkpoints did not need

evals.prompt: The project-archival branch touches both api and web. Before I review it I want to see how the two sides line up — is the frontend actually handling what the API now sends?
evals.expected_output: A review map that follows archived_at from ProjectSerializer through the JSON to the TypeScript type and names what the diff does not state: the wire key is archived_at while the client type declares archivedAt with no transform between them and no null in its type, the archive endpoint can return 422 and nothing in web/ handles it, and web/src/queries/selectableProjects.ts filters the list without knowing archival exists. Each is a judgment the reviewer has to make, so each is a checkpoint rather than a paragraph.
expectations: check.rb passes, including that selectableProjects and archivedAt are both named

The contract disagreement is a checkpoint whose chain shows the hops from serializer to component, with the mismatch carried on the edge that crosses from JSON to the declared type rather than written into a node as a sentence
Every claim about intent that is not visible in the diff carries an evidence tier
No excerpt quotes a whole file or every hunk of one, and none quotes a generated file, a lockfile or a pure rename
No two excerpts are near-duplicates of each other — structurally identical code quoted twice teaches once and costs twice

The nullable/non-null mismatch, the unhandled 422 and selectableProjects each have exactly one canonical explanation; later mentions are one-sentence references that add a purpose rather than repeating one
Where prose would narrate what a guard or serializer does, the page shows the lines and states the implication instead
Deploy ordering appears only if it is a judgment for this diff, and then as a checkpoint naming a safe order — not as a section that exists because the two sides ship separately
The impact section carries one to three paths and each ends at something a user or an operator would see, not at another function

evals.prompt: can you do a review map for the fix-typo branch
evals.expected_output: No published page. The skill says the diff is a one-line typo fix in the README, that a review map would be ceremony, and offers to stop.
expectations: No artifact is published
The response says plainly that this diff does not need a review map, and offers to stop rather than asking permission to continue
It does not emit sections, checkpoints or figures for material the diff never touches
It does not offer a source excerpt of the one changed line as a consolation deliverable

evals.prompt: I've got a review slot on project-archival in about twenty minutes and I don't know the branch at all. Can you get me oriented?
evals.expected_output: Staged delivery, which is the default and is not requested here. A URL arrives early, carrying the masthead and What changed, a build banner, and pending markers for the parts this diff earns. It fills in at that same URL, and section 02 fills in one checkpoint at a time — each pending checkpoint carrying its question, so a reader learns what the judgments are before any of them is written.
evals.check: snapshot the page file right after the first publish, then run both: evals/check.rb --draft --page <stage-1 snapshot> --repo <fixture> --base HEAD~1 ; evals/check.rb --final --page <final page> --repo <fixture> --base HEAD~1
expectations: check.rb --draft passes on the first published state: banner present, the sentence about a pending part not being a finding intact, pending markers for the parts still coming
check.rb --final passes on the last state: no banner, no pending markers, coverage gate green
The URL reported at the end is the same one reported at the start — one artifact, not two
The page title and favicon are identical across every stage
The first publish lands before any checkpoint is written, not after

Section 02 is delivered per checkpoint: an intermediate state shows at least one written checkpoint beside at least one <section class="cp"> stub, and a stub's line of substance is its question rather than 'coming soon'
No checkpoint stub survives on the final page — the per-checkpoint markers go with the banner, not after it

The impact section arrives before the checkpoints, because it is what tracing consumers produces; a page that publishes it last has staged in procedure order rather than in the order the material becomes available
The user is told the URL once, with a note that it will fill in — not re-pasted on every republish

evals.prompt: Someone reported they can't log in — the browser just bounces until it gives up. The fix is on fix/steward-redirect-loop and it's four lines, but I don't trust that it's only four lines. Can you map what this actually changes? Don't skimp — I want every section.
evals.expected_output: A review map for a server-rendered monolith, where what a checkpoint has to describe is the global before_action chain and the set of redirect destinations, not a JSON contract. Citations are plain text with the reason stated once — rung 3, because nothing is pushed. The four planted findings are judgments, and the agenda should reach them: the sibling steward? guards forty lines below the change, the eligibility filter disagreeing with User.recommendable about the same population, switch_to_free! holding only by conjunction, and test/test_helper.rb completing every test user's profile so a green suite cannot see any of it.
expectations: check.rb passes: coverage gate over seven paths, no severity chips, no verdict language, evidence tiers used, three theme states, and all four planted findings named
No GitHub permalink is emitted anywhere, and the reason is stated once in the masthead rather than left as a puzzle
Affected-but-unchanged entries in the same file as a changed hunk are found and cited by line, not skipped because the file already appears in the inventory

The page states that no test in the suite can observe the profile-setup interception, and attributes it to test/test_helper.rb rather than to a missing test. That is a checkpoint about the evidence, not a Tests subsection
The switch_to_free! guard is explained as holding by conjunction — has_paid_subscription? requires plan_active? — and not merely asserted to be safe or unsafe

Four findings do not become four checkpoints by default: where two share one judgment they are merged, and a checkpoint that cannot be merged is named in a clause of its nearest neighbour rather than added as a sixth
A guard chain is a strong candidate for a figure.chain, and the one drawn carries no affected-unchanged node — the reach into the sibling guards is an impact path and belongs in section 04
The absence of a separate client package is stated once, and distinguished from having no client at all — the client here is the browser and the ERB views in the same repository
Nothing claims the loop is fixed for users who already hold the column; the page says no migration touches existing rows and that the repository cannot say how many are affected
No sentence grades the change, scores its risk, or recommends approving it — including in the checkpoint whose judgment is unresolved
